blocks.purpose: Targets the classic mistake of labeling a subordinate-clause fragment (starting with because/when/although) as complete, with tempting flawed options.

options.text: Complete — it has a subject (the bells) and a verb (rang), so it is a full sentence.
options.whyNot: It does have those parts, but the word Although turns the whole thing into a dependent clause. A dependent clause leaning on nothing is still a fragment.

options.text: Fragment — Although makes this a dependent clause, so the thought is incomplete on its own.
options.whyNot: Correct. The subordinating word stops the clause from standing alone; it needs an independent clause to attach to.

options.text: Fixable with just a comma — write: Although the bells rang, and leave it there.
options.whyNot: A comma cannot finish a dependent clause. You must add an independent clause, not just punctuation.

data.decisionPrompt: Rewrite the broken sentence so it is fully correct. You may add punctuation, a joining word (FANBOYS), or a subordinating word — and you may split it into more than one sentence if that is cleanest.

misconception.detail: Fixing the fragment or the splice with only a comma does not work. A comma alone cannot join independent clauses (that creates a splice), and no punctuation can complete a dependent clause on its own. Use a period, semicolon, or comma + FANBOYS for the clauses, and attach the dependent clause to a complete sentence.
misconception.title: The comma-only trap

rule.name: The Repair Rules
rule.statement: A complete sentence needs a subject, a finite verb, and a complete thought. Fix a fused run-on with a period, a semicolon, a comma + FANBOYS, or a subordinating word. Never join two independent clauses with only a comma.

data.scenarioBody: A student submitted this sentence to the school paper: Although the stage was crowded the soloist found her spotlight, she sang the final verse the audience fell silent. Two problems are hiding in it: a fused run-on, and a subordinate clause left standing alone. Your job is to rebuild the sentence so it is fully correct — and say which repair rules you used.

targetAnswer.decision: Although the stage was crowded, the soloist found her spotlight. She sang the final verse, and the audience fell silent. (Also correct: use a semicolon — 'She sang the final verse; the audience fell silent.')
targetAnswer.rationale: The original hides three problems. 'Although the stage was crowded' is a subordinate-clause fragment standing alone, so it must be attached to a complete sentence with a comma after 'crowded.' 'The soloist found her spotlight, she sang the final verse' is a comma splice: a comma alone cannot join two independent clauses. Fix it by starting a new sentence with a period, or keep it in one sentence with a semicolon or a comma + FANBOYS. Finally, 'the final verse the audience fell silent' is a fused run-on with no punctuation at all, so it needs a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS conjunction (here 'and' works well).

checks.prompt: What exactly makes a group of words a fragment?
checks.answer: A fragment is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.
checks.rationale: The deciding step: a complete sentence needs a subject, a finite verb, and a complete thought, so a fragment is defined by missing one of those three — not by length or its first word.
checks.hint: Recall the three requirements of a complete sentence — a fragment is missing one of them.
choices: A fragment is missing a subject, a verb, or a complete thought.
A fragment is a very short sentence with only a few words.
A fragment is any sentence that starts with a subordinating word.
A fragment is a sentence with more than one subject.
checks.focus: Definitions of complete sentence, fragment, run-on, comma splice

checks.prompt: Into the box. In the final minute, kicked the ball over the fence.
checks.answer: Fragment — there is no subject: who was kicking?
checks.rationale: Kicked is a finite verb and the thought is complete, but there is no subject telling us who kicked — so it fails one of the three requirements and is a fragment.
checks.hint: Check the three requirements one at a time. Kicked is a verb — but whose foot did the kicking?
choices: Fragment — there is no subject: who was kicking?
Complete — the ball receives the action of kicked.
Complete — kicked is a finite verb, so it counts.
Fragment — a sentence cannot start with the word In.
checks.focus: Identifying a fragment missing a subject

checks.prompt: Is this a complete sentence or a fragment? Answer with one word. When the lights went out during the play.
checks.rationale: The subordinating word When makes the clause dependent, and a dependent clause with nothing attached lacks a complete thought — so it is a fragment.
checks.hint: Because is a subordinating word. Can a clause it starts with stand alone?

checks.prompt: The concert ended the crowd sang the last chorus together. What is the error?
checks.answer: Run-on — the second clause is fused on with no punctuation at all.
checks.rationale: The crowd sang... is an independent clause attached with no punctuation whatsoever between the clauses — that fusion is the definition of a run-on, distinct from a comma splice.
checks.hint: Look closely at what sits between the two clauses. Is there anything there?
choices: Run-on — the second clause is fused on with no punctuation at all.
Comma splice — a comma sits between the two clauses.
Complete — the semicolon joins the two clauses correctly.
Fragment — the second part has no subject.
checks.focus: Spotting a run-on in running text

checks.prompt: The museum closed at six, we had forty minutes left. One word of punctuation fixes this while keeping both clauses closely linked. Which single punctuation mark is the best fix here? (One word.)
checks.rationale: The clauses are closely related and the sentence needs no added conjunction, so the semicolon is the best single-mark fix; a comma alone would still be a splice.
checks.hint: The two clauses are closely related, and you want the punctuation alone to do the joining — no extra word needed.
checks.focus: Choosing the correct fix (semicolon vs comma + FANBOYS)

checks.prompt: Fix this broken sentence in full: Because the rehearsal ran late. The stage crew worked until midnight. (Write the whole corrected sentence, joining it into one.)
checks.answer: Because the rehearsal ran late, the stage crew worked until midnight.
checks.rationale: Because... is a subordinate-clause fragment; attaching it to the independent clause with a comma makes one correct complex sentence.
accepts: Because the rehearsal ran late, the stage crew worked until midnight.
